primaryStatutoryAuthority.description: Adult conviction sealing/expungement (§ 2953.32): an eligible offender applies to the sentencing court (or a court of common pleas for an out-of-state/federal conviction) unless excluded by § 2953.32(A); the court checks timing, pending cases, rehabilitation, prosecutor/victim objections, and whether the person's interest outweighs legitimate government needs.

Multiple charges from the same act (§ 2953.61): if a person was charged with two or more offenses from the same act and at least one charge has a different final disposition, they generally cannot seal/expunge only part of the record until they can seal/expunge all related charges (limited traffic exception). Ask for every charge and disposition before routing.

counselFlags: Sealing is not erasure: Ohio has BOTH sealing and expungement, and they are not the same. Sealing makes the record private from most employers, landlords, schools, and the general public but does not erase it (certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges, and police may still see it). Do not say 'completely gone from everywhere.'

The single most important Ohio disclosure: on § 2953.32 relief, BCI keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase; never describe the record as completely gone from everywhere.

Registry build blocker: the full text of ORC 2953.32 was not read at source by the controlling review; the waiting periods and exclusions are the review's, corroborated by the Franklin County Law Library guides, and the section must be read before any tier ships.

Registry build blocker: Ohio publishes no statewide mandatory form and each court maintains its own application; whether any county's local application deviates from the statutory content requirements is unresolved. The drafted content is transcribed onto the sentencing court's own application.
Registry release blocker: the exact terms of the third-degree-felony counting rule (whether a person with more than one third-degree felony is barred) are unresolved.

Relief is discretionary: the court checks timing and pending cases, considers rehabilitation and prosecutor and victim objections, and weighs the applicant's interest against legitimate governmental needs; the prosecutor is notified at least 60 days before the hearing and may object at least 30 days before it.
'Sentence' does not include payment of court costs, so unpaid court costs do not delay eligibility — a common and expensive misunderstanding worth telling participants explicitly.
Companion-charge trap (ORC 2953.61): an incident whose companion charge has a different final disposition cannot be partially sealed until all related charges can be cleared together.
SB 288 removed the 'eligible offender' definition and the numeric cap from ORC 2953.31; any counting-caps logic inherited from pre-2023 Ohio is wrong.

Excluded categories include traffic-chapter offenses (Chapters 4506/4507/4510/4511/4549), felony offenses of violence that are not sexually oriented offenses, sexually oriented offenses committed while subject to Chapter 2950 registration, victim-under-13 offenses (except nonsupport), theft in office, F1/F2 felonies, and M1/M2 domestic violence.
The applicant signs the application; notarization is not identified by the source and local practice may require it. Confirm any verification requirement with the clerk of the sentencing court.
Fees: fifty dollars unless indigent, plus a possible local court fee of not more than fifty dollars; indigency excuses the application fee.

Notice is the court's act: on a § 2953.32 application the court sets the hearing and the prosecutor is notified at least 60 days before it and may object at least 30 days before it. The applicant does not serve anyone, and the prosecutor's position is never asserted in the application.

waitingPeriods.condition: Minor misdemeanour, measured from final discharge
Felony of the fourth or fifth degree, measured from final discharge
One or two felonies of the third degree, measured from final discharge
Soliciting improper compensation under ORC 2921.43, measured from final discharge
A person formerly subject to Chapter 2950 registration
waitingPeriods.duration: 5 years after the registration requirements end or terminate
none. Any time after the forfeiture entry

exclusions: Offences under the traffic and motor vehicle chapters, being Chapters 4506, 4507, 4510, 4511 and 4549, or substantially similar municipal ordinances, which puts OVI outside the scheme.
A felony offence of violence that is not a sexually oriented offence.
A sexually oriented offence committed while subject to Chapter 2950 registration.
An offence where the victim was under 13, except nonsupport under ORC 2919.21.
Any felony of the first or second degree.
Domestic violence under ORC 2919.25 as a misdemeanour of the first or second degree, or a substantially similar municipal ordinance.
A felony of the third degree where the person has too many other convictions under the statute's third-degree-felony counting rule.
Any incident where a companion charge from the same act has a different final disposition, until all related charges can be cleared together. ORC 2953.61.
